words: I bought the things I needed.

The commonest noun in Korean, and it stands in for whatever you have not named. 제 것 is *mine*; 먹을 것 is *something to eat*. In speech it shrinks to 거 — 이거, 그거, 저거 — which is why beginners meet the short form first.
Korean uses one word where English uses two: 있다 is both to be somewhere and to have. 책상에 책이 있어요 is the book is on the desk; 시간이 있어요 is I have time. Its opposite is 없다.
To do — and the engine of Korean vocabulary. Attach it to a noun and you have a verb: 공부 study becomes 공부하다 to study, 사랑 love becomes 사랑하다. Hundreds of verbs are built this way.
A car. The same syllable is also the word for tea, so 차를 마셔요 is I drink tea and 차를 타요 is I get in a car. The verb tells you which one it is.
There is money in the wallet.
Speech — words, what someone says. The same syllable is also the word for a horse, and 말 also ends 한국말, the Korean language. Nothing separates them in writing; 말을 하다 is to speak, 말을 타다 is to ride.
Time in general, and also the counter for hours: 두 시간 is two hours. Do not confuse it with 시, which is the o'clock hour — 두 시 is two o'clock, a different thing entirely.
The sun rises in the morning.

Three common words are spelled 네. This one is "yes". The others are "your" (네 책, your book) and the native number four before a counter (네 개, four things). Context separates them; nothing in the spelling does.

A dog — and, spelled the same, the counter for things: 사과 두 개, two apples; 세 개 주세요, three please. The counter takes native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋 become 한, 두, 세 in front of it). You will meet the counter far more often than the animal.
Two other words are spelled 분. One is the polite way of counting people — 세 분, three people, said of guests or elders. The other means anger, as in 분이 풀리다. Only the sentence tells them apart.
I wash my body every day.
I wrote my name on the back of the notebook.
The eye. Spelled identically to the word for snow, and in careful speech the two are told apart by length: the snow 눈 is drawn out, the eye 눈 is short. Most speakers rely on context instead.

The head — and also the hair on it: 머리를 잘랐어요 means I got a haircut, and 머리를 감아요 is washing your hair, not your head. 머리가 아파요 is a headache; 머리가 좋아요 means clever. When you need the hair specifically, 머리카락 is the strand-by-strand word.
A leg — yours, a table's, a chair's. The same word also means a bridge, which is why 다리를 건너요 is I cross a bridge and not something anatomical.
The class finishes at two o'clock.

The hour takes the native numbers — 한 시, 두 시, 세 시 — and the minute takes the Sino-Korean ones: 세 시 십 분, ten past three. Getting the two the wrong way round is the classic beginner slip, and it is heard immediately.
Let's meet in front of the shop.
I opened the gift I got for my birthday.

An ㄹ-final verb: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ and ㅅ, so it is 압니다 (formal), 아세요? (do you know?) and 아는 사람 (someone I know), but 알아요, 알고 and 알면 keep it. 알겠어요 is how you say understood, OK — a phrase you will hear constantly. Its opposite, 모르다, is 르-irregular: 몰라요.
I wash my hands before eating.

Before, in time. Several other words are written 전: 전쟁 is war and shortens to 전, 전기 is electricity, and 전 on a menu is a savoury pancake. As a standalone word before a verb it is the time one — 먹기 전에, before eating.

Cooked rice, and by extension a meal of any kind: 밥 먹었어요? (have you eaten?) is an everyday greeting, and 밥 먹으러 가요 means let's go eat, whatever the food. Uncooked rice is 쌀, and the plant in the field is 벼. 식사 is the more formal word for a meal.
a little, and a softener in requests

Short for 조금, *a little* — but half its work is softening. Dropped into a request it takes the edge off: 도와주세요 is *help me*, 좀 도와주세요 is closer to *could you help me*. Korean speakers use it constantly for exactly that reason.
Please do it one more time.
Please take the medicine after eating.

Well, and much more: 잘 먹었습니다 (thank you for the meal, literally I ate well), 잘 잤어요? (did you sleep well?), 잘 가요 (goodbye to someone leaving), 잘 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure). With 하다 it becomes 잘하다, to be good at: 한국어를 잘해요. Its opposite is 못, badly or unable.
Health is the most important thing.
I buy vegetables at the market.
A fire broke out on the mountain.
I go to the sea in summer.
I lived in the countryside when I was young.

A time, in the sense of when: 어릴 때 (when I was little), 밥 먹을 때 (when eating), 그때 (at that time), 방학 때 (during the holidays). It follows a noun directly or a verb with -ㄹ/을: 갈 때, when going; 먹을 때, when eating. For a duration or a clock time, use 시간 and 시 instead.
The two of us are going together.
There is a lot of work today.
Work, or a thing that has to be done. The same syllable is the Sino-Korean one — 일 번, number one — and it is the day in 일요일, Sunday, and 삼 일, three days.
There are many stars at night.
Night. Spelled the same as the word for a chestnut, which is a common autumn snack in Korea, so 밤을 먹어요 and 밤에 자요 are about very different things.
The opposite of 이다. It takes 이/가 on the thing being denied, not 을/를: 학생이 아니에요, never 학생을 아니에요. A beginner who learns that one pattern can negate any noun sentence in Korean.
I draw a picture on paper.
There is a hat on the bag.
It is so spicy that I cannot eat it.

Korean has two negatives and they say different things. 안 is *I do not*; 못 is *I cannot*. 안 먹어요 means you are choosing not to eat; 못 먹어요 means something is stopping you. A noun spelled the same way, 못, is a nail.
It snows a lot in winter.
There are many people on the street.
I wash the rice and cook it.
I boiled an egg in the morning.
I hang a picture on the wall.
To get on or into anything that carries you — a bus, a bike, a lift. Two other very common verbs share the spelling: 타다 also means to burn, and to stir something into a drink.
I put a little salt in the soup.
I get up in the morning.
I meet my friend at a cafe.
Mr or Ms, after a name

Attached to a given name it is polite and friendly between equals: 민수 씨. Attached to a family name alone — 김 씨 — it sounds distant or even curt, so use the given name. To a superior, use their title instead: 부장님, 선생님.
Nice to meet you for the first time.
The wind is cool in autumn.
There is a book on the desk.
My daughter is learning the piano.
I want to become a doctor.

To become. It is also the everyday word for something working or being allowed: 안 돼요 means that will not do, and 다 됐어요 means it is finished. You will hear those far more often than the dictionary sense.
I go to the library after class.
I write a letter to my mother.
Really, truly — an intensifier before an adjective, as in 정말 좋아요. On its own, with a rise at the end, 정말? is the one-word question really?, which is how you will hear it most.

Originally too, excessively — 너무 커요, it's too big — and in everyday speech also just very: 너무 좋아요, I love it; 너무 맛있어요, really delicious. Both are natural. For a plain, neutral very, 아주 and 정말 are the safer choices in writing.
I bought bread. And I bought milk too.
to be visible, to be seen
I want to go to Korea.

To want to — but it never stands alone. It attaches to a verb with 고: 가고 싶어요 (I want to go), 먹고 싶어요 (I want to eat). For wanting a thing, Korean still uses a verb: 커피를 마시고 싶어요, I want (to drink) coffee. About a third person it becomes 싶어하다: 동생이 가고 싶어해요, my little brother wants to go.
There is a big dragon in the picture.

Heart and mind at once — feelings, intentions, the inner self, not the organ (that is 심장). Three phrases carry most of its use: 마음에 들어요 (I like it, literally it enters my heart), 마음이 아파요 (it hurts, emotionally) and 마음대로 (as you please). 마음이 따뜻하다 is warm-hearted.
I know many countries of the world.
Please throw it in the bin.

A ㅎ-irregular adjective: the ㅎ drops before a vowel and the vowel fronts, giving 그래요 (that's right, I see) and 그랬어요, and it drops before ㄴ too: 그런 사람, that kind of person. 그렇고 and 그렇지만 keep it. 이렇다 (like this), 저렇다 (like that over there) and 어떻다 (how) form a family with it — 이래요, 저래요, 어때요. The adverb 그렇게 means so, in that way.
The flower in the pot died because it was not watered.
To write. The same verb also means to use something, to wear a hat or glasses on the head, and — as an adjective — to taste bitter. Four everyday meanings, one spelling.
I have a lot of worries.
It is warm in the daytime.
I put the milk in the refrigerator.
a hen's egg, the native word
I eat an egg in the morning.
I put the bag on the floor.
That was truly like a miracle.
I peeled the apple with a knife.
The office is on the third floor.
The book is under the desk.
an egg laid by a bird or a fish

Thank you, in the warmer of the two everyday forms: 고마워요 to friends and people you are on easy terms with, 고맙습니다 more formally. 감사합니다 means the same and is the safer choice with strangers, staff and elders. Both are ㅂ-irregular in the polite form — 고마워요, not 고맙어요.

Still, or not yet: with a negative it means not yet — 아직 안 왔어요, they haven't come yet; 아직 몰라요, I don't know yet — and with a plain verb it means still, 아직 자요, still asleep. Its counterpart is 벌써 (already, sooner than expected); 이미 is already in the neutral sense.
I stamped it with a seal.
To press something down onto a surface: a seal, a stamp, a fingerprint. The same verb covers taking a photograph — 사진을 찍다 — and dipping food into a sauce, all three from the one idea of pressing.

Textbooks list 당신 as polite "you", but in real speech it is mostly used between spouses — or, said to a stranger, it sounds confrontational. Koreans usually avoid "you" altogether: they use the person's name or title (선생님, 사장님) instead. Use 당신 with care.
It's raining, so I'm not going.

Already, with a note of surprise: sooner than you expected. 벌써 다 끝났어요? — it's over already? 벌써 열두 시예요, it's twelve already. When there is no surprise, Korean uses 이미: 이미 알고 있었어요, I already knew. The opposite is 아직, still or not yet.
There are many students in the classroom.
The children are looking for treasure.
When I am sick I eat rice porridge.
I pour water into the cup.
Korean's native numbers change shape before a counter. 하나 둘 셋 넷 become 한 두 세 네: 하나 on its own, 한 개 for one item. 두 is that form of 둘, and it never stands alone.
I come from the United States.
a price as a stated figure
The price is higher than expected.
The one sibling word that does not change with the speaker: anyone younger is 동생, whoever is talking. Add a syllable when you need the sex — 남동생 for a younger brother, 여동생 for a younger sister.
I wait for the bus at the stop.
There is a convenience store in front of my house.
Please tell me how to use it.
I added a little spring onion to the soup.
My mother works at a hospital.
I don't know the meaning of this word.
I travelled during the school holidays.
The cat is under the bed.
Here 열 is the native Korean ten, the one you use for counting things — 열 개, ten of them. A different 열 means a fever, and the verb 열다 means to open. Same two letters, three unrelated words.
There was the sound of a beast in the forest.
Let's meet at the entrance of the building.
My tongue hurts, so I can't eat.
Let me ask just one thing.
Also the name of the aubergine, and also a branch of a tree. As a counter it is what you reach for with things you can list: 두 가지 방법, two ways; 세 가지 이유, three reasons.
I dry my hands with a towel.
You can hear birdsong in the forest.

To like is a verb in Korean, and 좋다 (to be good) is an adjective, so the particle changes: 커피를 좋아해요 (I like coffee) but 커피가 좋아요 (coffee is good, I like coffee). Beginners mix the two; 를 goes with 좋아하다 only. 싫어하다 (to dislike) pairs with 싫다 in exactly the same way.
I add tofu and make soup.
I watch television in the living room.
Please stand at the end of the queue.
The capital of Korea is Seoul.
The capital of a country. A separate 수도 means the mains water supply — 수도꼭지 is a tap, 수도 요금 is the water bill. The two are told apart entirely by what is around them.
I have a favour to ask.
We took a boat to the island.
What is the title of this book?
I went to see the flowers.
A bee landed on the flower.
A bee. Two other words are spelled 벌: a punishment, and the counter for a set of clothes — 옷 한 벌, one outfit.
I went shopping at the weekend.
The spacecraft rose into the sky.
I eat a lot of vegetables.
Don't forget to bring the passport.
My stomach hurt, so I went to the hospital.
The stomach. Two other common words are spelled 배: a boat, and a pear. 배가 아파요 is my stomach hurts, 배를 타요 is I get on a boat, and 배를 먹어요 is I eat a pear.
The insect. Korean writes the city Paris the same way, so 파리에 갔어요 means I went to Paris while 파리가 있어요 means there is a fly. Nothing but the sentence tells them apart.
A young woman is asking for directions.

A young unmarried woman — but as a way of *addressing* a stranger it has gone sour, and many women find it rude or belittling. Use it about someone, not to them; to get a stranger's attention say 저기요.
We're going on a picnic tomorrow.
I put the book on the desk.
It rained, so I bought an umbrella.
What kind of colour do you like?
There is a tree between the two houses.
I had a strange dream last night.
I wash my face in the morning.

A ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so it is 들어요 and 들었어요, but 듣고 and 듣습니다 keep the ㄷ. That makes 들어요 look like the verb 들다 (to hold, to lift) — the context tells them apart. 묻다 (to ask) and 걷다 (to walk) change the same way.
I wash the strawberries and eat them.
I bought a book at the bookshop.
It is a special gift to me.
I draw a picture with a pencil.
My older brother bought me a meal.
A man's word for an older brother. A woman would say 오빠 for the same person. Like 오빠, it extends to a close older man who is not family at all.
I put rice in the bowl.

Korean picks the word for a sibling by the speaker's own gender: a woman calls her older brother 오빠, a man calls him 형. It is also used for an older man a woman is close to, which is why you hear it far outside families.
I play football with my friend.
I worked in the laboratory all day.
This ring is made of gold.
Gold, the metal. The same syllable also means a scratched or drawn line — 금이 갔어요 is it has cracked — and it opens 금요일, Friday.
The smell of cigarettes soaked into my clothes.
I borrowed a book from the library.
The dog is holding a bone in its mouth.
I eat one banana in the morning.
We wrap rice in laver and eat it.
The thin dried seaweed eaten with rice. The same syllable is the commonest Korean family name, and it is also steam rising off something hot — 김이 나요, it is steaming.
My younger sibling is very kind.

Years of age, counted with native numbers: 스무 살 (twenty), 서른 살 (thirty), 몇 살이에요? (how old are you?). Note the changed forms in front of it — 한 살, 두 살, 세 살, 스무 살. Spelled the same, 살 is also flesh or skin (살이 쪘어요, I put on weight); the number in front tells you which.
The scenery here is really lovely.
Korean popular song, as a category — K-pop is 가요. It is spelled exactly like 가요 "goes / is going", the polite present of 가다, so the sentence around it decides which one you are reading.
At the weekend I just stayed home.
to do well, to be good at
I got out of bed at the sound of the alarm.
I was glad to hear the news.
The four of us are one team.
A glass of cold water, please.

A 르-irregular adjective: before 아/어 the 르 doubles its ㄹ onto the syllable before, so it is 달라요 and 달랐어요, while 다르고 and 다릅니다 are regular. 빠르다 (fast), 모르다 (to not know) and 부르다 (to call) change the same way — 빨라요, 몰라요, 불러요. It takes 와/과 or 하고 for what something differs from: 저와 달라요.
to give a hand, to help out
a mobile phone, the formal word
This is the first time for such a thing.
I prepared the meeting materials in advance.
We grilled beef and ate it.
I drink tea instead of coffee.
By the way, what is this?
to be left over, to remain
I saw a mouse in the kitchen.
I write my name in the notebook.
There were many stones on the path, so we were careful.
I put the book in the bag.
A lot of laundry has piled up.
This shop is famous for its bread.
I haven't been able to sleep well lately.
My son goes to middle school.
We went to the beach in the summer.
I did the dishes after dinner.
A bird flies in the sky.
They have a talent for drawing.
By the way, what time is it now?
Please give me your contact details.
I received a good proposal from the company.
